core_rules.reason: A topic label written in place of a proposition cannot be reviewed, and is the most common first mistake in a new claim.
Bundled properties are the characteristic output of a single-sentence instruction such as "argue that X is safe and secure".
Authors and language models both tend to write the whole branch into one claim rather than using the structure.
Unbounded qualifiers enter at writing time and are expensive to bound afterwards, once the branch below depends on the wording.
Chained lifecycle steps look like one claim while needing several evidence sets, and are easiest to separate before support is attached.
Element role misuse is a writing-time choice; a tool can prevent it more cheaply than a review can correct it.
Sub-claims added under a claim with no reasoning step is the characteristic shape of generated argument.
Scope and dependencies written into claim text are hard to separate later, once other elements refer to the claim.
A claim written with no intended evidence path should be marked undeveloped when it is written, not discovered unsupported at review.
Naming the document rather than the fact is a writing habit, and it overstates what the artifact shows.
Citation precision is cheap while the author still knows which section they meant.
A live source cited without a fixed version silently invalidates the argument later, and the fixing information is available at writing time.
Assumptions are easiest to state while the author still knows what they were assuming.
An unstated dependency is invisible to review by definition, so it has to be caught where it is introduced.
Support that restates its parent is a common filler pattern when an author or a model has no real support to offer.
Arguing from absence reads as evidence and is not, and it is written most often when the search basis is not to hand.
Signposting an element's role costs nothing while writing it and cannot be recovered from the text afterwards.
Promotional wording is introduced at writing time and always weakens rather than strengthens the argument.

authoring_guidance.description: The SCCG subset a tool should deliver while an author or an AI agent is writing, rather than when a review is run. Every guideline still applies; this set names the rules that are most often broken at the moment of writing and short enough to carry in a system prompt, an editor hint, or an agent's session instructions.
authoring_guidance.usage: Render each rule from the guideline's short_rule field and cite its id. Do not paraphrase, and do not present this set as SCCG conformance; it is a delivery subset, not a reduced standard.

availability_states.meaning: The package is supplied and carries the data the profile expects.
The tool has no source for this package at all.
The tool has a source for this package and this case has nothing in it.
The data exists and was deliberately not shared with the review, for example by a consent or confidentiality decision.

document.purpose:
This document consolidates review guidance for safety cases into one
guideline-based review framework that can be cited during reviews.
document.title: Safety Case Core Guidelines

examples.bad: Brake monitor safety
examples.good: Brake monitor response time meets the defined acceptance criterion.
examples.problem: This is a topic label, not a falsifiable proposition. A reviewer cannot tell what would have to be true or false to accept or reject it.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case is built from claims that can be challenged, supported, or refuted. Statements that are merely labels, headings, slogans, or references are poor safety claims.
review_prompts: Could a reviewer tell what would make this claim false?
Is this a proposition, or only a topic label?
Is the claim understandable without extra interpretation?
guidelines.short_rule: State each claim as a short proposition a reviewer could judge true or false.
guidelines.statement: State each claim as a sentence that can in principle be shown true or false.
guidelines.title: Write each claim as a falsifiable proposition

detection_hints: Look for goal text that is a noun phrase or topic label rather than a proposition.
Look for goals lacking a verb expressing a property or a measurable condition.

repair.statement: Restate the claim as a proposition with a subject and an asserted property that could be shown false.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim text is a complete proposition that can be true or false. Candidate when the claim has no predicate asserting a property, or states a requirement in place of a proposition.

examples.bad: Planning software is safe and secure.
examples.good:
Planning software safety is acceptable.

And separately:

Planning software cybersecurity is acceptable.
examples.problem: The claim bundles two distinct properties (safety and cybersecurity) that need different evidence and review treatment, hiding missing decomposition.

guidelines.rationale: Bundled claims hide missing decomposition, make evidence assignment unclear, and produce review findings that are hard to localize.
review_prompts: Does the statement contain more than one property?
Would different evidence sets be needed for different parts of the claim?
Could one part of the statement be acceptable while another could fail?
guidelines.short_rule: Put one claim in one goal; separate properties that need different evidence.
guidelines.statement: Do not bundle multiple distinct properties, conclusions, or obligations into one goal.
guidelines.title: Put one main claim in one goal

detection_hints: Look for conjunctions linking distinct properties (safe and secure, complete and correct).
Look for goals where different properties would be supported by different evidence sets.

repair.statement: Split the bundled claim into one claim per property, each with its own support.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim asserts a single property or bundles several distinct properties. Candidate when two or more distinct property terms are joined by a conjunction within one claim; one property term alone is not a signal.

examples.bad: The product concept and system design, including faults, failures, interfaces, dependencies, degraded operation and transitions to safe states, are acceptably safe for operation within the defined ODD.
examples.good:
Claim: Design safety is acceptable.
Context: Applies within the defined ODD.
Reasoning: Break the design safety claim into safety-relevant design topics.
Sub-claims:
- Fault handling safety is acceptable.
- Failure response safety is acceptable.
- Safety-relevant interfaces are acceptable.
- Safety-relevant dependencies are acceptable.
- Degraded operation safety is acceptable.
- Transitions to safe states are acceptable.
examples.problem: The claim packs scope, decomposition topics, and caveats into one sentence, hiding the argument structure that should be visible through context, strategy, and sub-claims.

guidelines.rationale: When a claim contains the whole story, reviewers cannot clearly see what is being claimed, what constrains the claim, and how the argument is intended to proceed. In GSN, that information should be visible in the structure, not hidden inside one sentence.
review_prompts: Is the goal text trying to describe both the claim and its decomposition?
Is scope that should be in context embedded in the claim text?
Are included topics listed in the claim instead of being expressed as sub-claims?
Would the argument become clearer if the parent claim were shortened and the included topics moved into strategy and child claims?
guidelines.short_rule: Keep claim text short: scope belongs in context, reasoning in a strategy, topics in sub-claims.
guidelines.statement: Do not pack argument structure, scope, decomposition topics, and caveats into a single claim. Keep the claim short, and express the rest through context, strategy, assumptions, and sub-claims.
guidelines.title: Avoid the essay-in-the-box

detection_hints: Look for claims that contain long comma-separated lists of topics.
Look for claim text that mixes scope, reasoning, caveats, and decomposition.
Look for phrases such as including, covering, considering, or with respect to introducing multiple subtopics.

repair.statement: Move scope and operating conditions out of the claim into context.
State the decomposition as a reasoning step instead of listing topics in the claim.
Make each listed topic a sub-claim below the claim.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim contains argument structure or scope that should be represented through context, strategy, assumptions, or sub-claims. Candidate when the claim exceeds the published word-count threshold, or an enumeration marker introduces a list of topics.
Check whether the claim lists child topics instead of making the decomposition visible in the argument structure.

thresholds.note: Claim text longer than this is a candidate for moving scope, reasoning, or listed topics out of the claim.

examples.bad: Software requirements development is acceptably safe.
examples.good: The process used to develop software functional requirements satisfies the defined safety assurance criteria.
examples.problem: Both the object (development activity vs. resulting requirements) and the property (safe vs. controlled) are ambiguous, so competent reviewers may interpret the claim differently.

guidelines.rationale: Ambiguous claims undermine review, traceability, and evidence relevance. This guideline directly supports UL 4600’s requirement to avoid substantive ambiguity in claims and arguments.
review_prompts: Could two competent reviewers understand the claim differently?
Is the object of the claim clear?
Is the property being claimed clear?
guidelines.short_rule: Word each claim so that two competent reviewers would read it the same way.
guidelines.statement: Write claims so that their meaning is clear enough that competent reviewers are likely to understand them in the same way.
guidelines.title: Avoid ambiguity and overloaded wording

detection_hints: Look for ambiguous subjects or properties (e.g. development is safe).
Look for claim text whose object or measured property is unclear.

repair.statement: Reword the claim so that its subject and asserted property have one reading.
Define the ambiguous term once, and let the claim use the definition.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether competent reviewers would interpret the claim consistently. A marker hit is a prompt to examine the claim's subject and asserted property, not a finding on its own.

examples.bad: The monitor provides timely mitigation.
examples.good: Upon detection of condition C4, the monitor initiates minimum risk maneuver entry within the defined threshold.
examples.problem: "Timely" is an unbounded evaluative qualifier; without a defined threshold or condition it cannot be reviewed consistently.

guidelines.rationale: Terms such as safe, timely, effective, normal, robust, all, every, and never can sound stronger or broader than the argument actually shows unless they are properly bounded.
review_prompts: Is the term bounded by context, lower-level argument, or linked criteria?
If safe is used, is it clear what safety judgment is being claimed at this level?
Is the scope of all, every, or never explicitly defined?
Would the claim remain reviewable if read on its own?
guidelines.short_rule: Bound every evaluative or universal qualifier in the claim, its context, or a defined term.
guidelines.statement: Do not leave broad evaluative terms or universal qualifiers unbounded. This includes terms such as safe, timely, effective, normal, robust, all, every, and never.
guidelines.title: Bound vague and universal qualifiers

detection_hints: Look for unbounded evaluative terms: safe, robust, effective, timely, normal.
Look for universal qualifiers without scope: all, every, never, always.

repair.statement: Define the qualifier once as a project term carrying its bound.
State the bound as context on the claim.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether evaluative or universal qualifiers in the claim are bounded by context or measurable criteria. Candidate when an unbounded evaluative term or universal qualifier appears and no bounding marker is present in the claim, its context, or a term it uses.

examples.bad: All identified hazards have been mitigated and validated.
examples.good:
Parent claim: Hazards are acceptably addressed.
Sub-claims:
- Hazards are identified.
- Defined mitigations are implemented.
- Validation evidence is sufficient.
examples.problem: The claim chains identification, implementation, and validation steps into one sentence; each step needs different evidence and a different review question.

guidelines.rationale: These are different claim types with different evidence and different review questions.
review_prompts: Is this claim actually several claims chained together?
Would different teams or documents support different parts?
Should the branch be decomposed before evidence is attached?
guidelines.short_rule: Do not chain identification, implementation, and validation in one claim; decompose them.
guidelines.statement: Do not combine identification, adequacy, implementation, validation, and sufficiency in one claim unless the claim is intentionally kept at a higher level and the need for later decomposition is explicit
guidelines.title: Do not mix different logical steps in one claim

detection_hints: Look for claims that chain identification + implementation + validation in one sentence.

repair.statement: Separate the chained steps into sub-claims carrying one logical step each.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim mixes identification, adequacy, implementation, validation, and sufficiency steps. Candidate when two or more lifecycle step verbs appear within one claim.

examples.bad: Claim: We argue that functional design safety is acceptable by decomposing into autonomy hazard topics, given that the ISO 26262 functional design scope applies and the project requires ISO 26262 compliance, supported by the functional safety requirements, safety mechanisms, and interfaces being defined.
examples.good:
Claim: Functional design safety is acceptable.
Reasoning: Break the claim down by autonomy hazard topic.
Scope: Functional design refers to the ISO 26262 functional design scope for the item.
Reason for including the claim: The project requires ISO 26262 compliance.
Sub-claims:
- Functional safety requirements are defined.
- Required safety mechanisms are defined.
- Safety-relevant interfaces are defined.
examples.problem: The single statement bundles claim, strategy, context, justification, and sub-claims; each element's role is hidden inside one sentence rather than carried by the structure.

guidelines.rationale: When one assurance case element is used to do another element's job, the argument becomes harder to inspect, review, and challenge.
review_prompts: Is a claim carrying reasoning that belongs in an argument, strategy, or warrant?
Is local scope or meaning hidden inside the claim instead of being made explicit?
Is a dependency or rationale hidden in claim or argument text?
Is an evidence reference being used as if it were a claim?
Is a justification being used as if it were support?
guidelines.short_rule: Let each element do its own job: claims assert, reasoning elements explain, evidence elements cite.
guidelines.statement: Use the assurance case structure to make each element's role clear. Claims state propositions to be established; argument elements explain the reasoning, decomposition approach, or inference rule; context and assumptions define scope and dependencies when needed; and evidence elements identify the artefacts or observations used as support.
guidelines.title: Let structure carry the argument

detection_hints: Look for goals containing reasoning verbs (we argue that, by decomposing).
Look for solutions phrased as claims rather than evidence references.
Look for assumptions or justifications buried in claim or strategy text.

repair.statement: Move each part of the text into the element whose role it plays.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each element is used for its intended role in the notation. Candidate when reasoning wording appears in a claim, when a claim's wording appears in an evidence element, or when rationale or scope is stated inside another element's text.

examples.bad: Perception, planning, control, timing, and interfaces are adequately addressed.
examples.good:
Claim: Autonomy function safety is acceptable.
Reasoning: Break the claim down by the autonomy function topics identified by UL 4600.
Reason for this breakdown: These topics match the autonomy-related topics that UL 4600 expects the safety case to address.
Sub-claims:
- ODD-related safety is acceptable.
- Sensing safety is acceptable.
- Perception safety is acceptable.
- Machine learning and AI technique safety is acceptable.
- Planning safety is acceptable.
- Prediction safety is acceptable.
- Trajectory and control safety is acceptable.
- Actuation safety is acceptable.
- Timing safety is acceptable.
examples.problem: The decomposition rule is not stated; a reviewer cannot tell why these specific children were chosen or whether they together support the parent.

guidelines.rationale: A hidden reasoning step is a common source of argument gaps.
review_prompts: Is the decomposition rule visible?
Would another reviewer derive the same child-claim set?
Does the strategy explain why these children support this parent?
guidelines.short_rule: State the decomposition or inference rule explicitly instead of leaving it to be inferred.
guidelines.statement: State how the parent claim is being decomposed or argued; do not make the reviewer infer the decomposition rule from wording alone.
guidelines.title: State the inference step explicitly

detection_hints: Look for branches with sub-claims but no strategy element explaining the decomposition rule.
Look for parent claims whose decomposition rule is implicit in the wording.

repair.statement: Insert an explicit reasoning step stating how the children support the claim.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each decomposition has an explicit reasoning step stating how children support the parent.

examples.bad: The braking controller is acceptably safe in Highway ODD during automated mode with valid localization and nominal interface timing.
examples.good:
Claim: Braking controller safety is acceptable.
Scope:
- Applies in Highway ODD.
- Applies in automated mode.
Dependencies:
- Valid localization available.
- Nominal interface timing conditions apply.
examples.problem: Scope (ODD, mode) and dependencies (localization, interface timing) are hidden inside the claim text instead of being represented as separate context and assumption elements.

guidelines.rationale: This keeps the claim interpretable and makes clear which information defines the claim's scope and meaning, and which conditions the argument depends on being true.
review_prompts: Is this text making the claim itself, defining the claim's scope, or stating a dependency that must hold?
Is any condition required for the claim to hold hidden in wording rather than made explicit?
Would the argument be clearer if scope, definitions, or dependencies were represented separately?
If context is included in claim text, is it deliberate, consistent, and necessary for the claim to be true or false?
guidelines.short_rule: Make scope, definitions, operating conditions, and dependencies explicit rather than implied.
guidelines.statement: Make scope, definitions, operating conditions, and dependencies explicit. Use separate context and assumption structures when supported by the notation or tool; where they must appear in claim text, write them deliberately and consistently rather than hiding them in ambiguous qualifiers.
guidelines.title: Use context and assumptions deliberately

detection_hints: Look for claim text containing scope phrases (in ODD X, during mode Y) or dependency phrases (with valid Z).

repair.statement: Move scope, definitions, and operating conditions into context.
State each condition the argument depends on as an assumption.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether scope and dependencies in claim text should be moved to context or assumption elements. Candidate when a scope phrase or dependency phrase marker appears inside claim text.

examples.bad: Upper-level claim: Detection timing meets the defined acceptance criterion.
examples.good:
Upper level: Functional design safety is acceptable.
Lower level: Sensing-related hazards are identified.
Evidence-facing level: Detection timing meets the defined acceptance criterion.
examples.problem: Using an evidence-facing precision at the top of the argument makes the upper level brittle and tied to specific measurements; upper-level claims should remain short and stable while leaf claims carry the precision needed to assess against evidence.

guidelines.rationale: Top-level claims need readability and stability. Lower-level claims need assessability.
review_prompts: Is a high-level claim overloaded with low-level detail?
Is a leaf claim too vague to assess against evidence?
Could the claim stay short because linked criteria already make it objective?
guidelines.short_rule: Keep upper-level claims short and stable; make evidence-facing claims precise enough to assess.
guidelines.statement: Keep upper-level claims short and stable; make evidence-facing claims precise enough to assess.
guidelines.title: Match claim precision to the level of the argument

detection_hints: Look for top-level claims overloaded with measurement detail.
Look for leaf claims too vague to compare with evidence.

repair.statement: Shorten an overloaded upper-level claim, or make a leaf claim precise enough to assess against its evidence.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether claim precision matches argument level.

examples.bad:
Parent claim: Software safety is acceptable.
Strategy: Argument by software component type.
Child claims:
- Application software safety is acceptable.
- Middleware software safety is acceptable.
examples.good:
Parent claim: Software safety is acceptable.
Context: Software in scope comprises application, middleware, platform, and driver layers.
Reasoning: Break the software safety claim down by software component type, covering all layers in scope.
Child claims:
- Application software safety is acceptable.
- Middleware software safety is acceptable.
- Platform software safety is acceptable.
- Driver software safety is acceptable.
examples.problem: The parent claim refers to all software, but the child claims silently narrow the scope to only part of the software. The branch appears complete while leaving other software out of scope without saying so.

guidelines.rationale: Silent redefinition can leave higher-level claims only partially supported while appearing complete.
review_prompts: Does a key term mean the same thing at parent and sub-claim levels?
Has scope narrowed without being stated?
Is inherited context still valid at this level?
guidelines.short_rule: Keep the object, scope, and terminology of a claim unchanged as the argument decomposes.
guidelines.statement: Do not silently redefine the object, scope, or meaning of key terms as the argument decomposes.
guidelines.title: Keep scope and terminology consistent across decomposition

detection_hints: Look for parent/child pairs where a key noun's scope changes silently.

repair.statement: State the full scope the decomposition is meant to cover as context on the parent.
Add the sub-claims needed to cover the parent's stated scope.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether key terms preserve scope across decomposition.

examples.bad: Perception performance is acceptable.
examples.good:
Claim: Perception performance is acceptable.
Definition: Perception performance refers to object detection, classification, and tracking performance as defined in Specification PER-01.
examples.problem: Perception performance is not defined, so different reviewers may understand different outputs, measures, or success conditions.

guidelines.rationale: This guideline is about whether the branch contains enough context at all. In GSN, claims are asserted in a specified context. A claim that lacks essential context can look stronger than intended or become hard to review consistently because different readers may supply different meanings or boundaries.
review_prompts: What must the reviewer know for this claim to be true or false?
Are key terms defined where needed?
Is any necessary scope or operating condition explicit?
Would two independent reviewers understand the claim in the same way?
guidelines.short_rule: Give each claim the context a reviewer needs to interpret its subject, scope, and key terms.
guidelines.statement: Provide the context needed for the reviewer to understand the claim’s subject, intended meaning, scope, operating conditions, and key definitions.
guidelines.title: Provide the context needed to interpret the claim

detection_hints: Look for claims using domain terms that are not defined in any linked context.

repair.statement: Add the context that defines the claim's subject, scope, and key terms.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim has enough linked context for consistent interpretation.

examples.bad: Planner safety is acceptable with valid localization and nominal interface timing.
examples.good:
Claim: Planner safety is acceptable.
Definition: Planner refers to the motion planning function defined in architecture element PLN-01.
Dependencies:
- Valid localization is available.
- Nominal interface timing conditions apply.
examples.problem: Qualifiers ("with valid localization", "nominal interface timing") are buried in the claim text, blurring the role of each element and making scope and dependency changes harder to see.

guidelines.rationale: This guideline is about placement, clarity, and maintainability. Hidden qualifiers blur element roles, make scope and dependency changes harder to see, and often create claims that are difficult to review and maintain.
review_prompts: Which words in this claim are qualifiers rather than the core assertion?
Are the qualifiers clear enough for review, or would they be better represented as context or assumptions?
Could the core claim remain stable if a configuration, interface condition, or dependency changed?
Are dependencies explicit and traceable rather than hidden inside readable but overloaded claim text?
guidelines.short_rule: Move qualifiers and dependency clauses out of claim text into context or assumptions.
guidelines.statement: Do not hide qualifiers, definitions, interface conditions, or dependency clauses in claim text in a way that obscures scope or support. Use separate context or assumption structures where available; otherwise make the qualifiers deliberate, clear, and consistently phrased.
guidelines.title: Make claim qualifiers explicit and maintainable

detection_hints: Look for connectives in claim text such as with, given, assuming, provided that, when.

repair.statement: Move qualifiers that define scope into context.
Move dependency clauses into an assumption.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether qualifying clauses in claim text should move to context or assumption elements. Candidate when a qualifier connective introduces a clause that bounds the claim rather than asserting it.

examples.bad:
Claim: Brake hazards are adequately addressed.
Rationale: The verification campaign passed all planned brake fault tests.
examples.good:
Claim: Brake hazards are adequately addressed.
Sub-claims:
- Brake hazards are identified.
- Mitigations for identified brake hazards are implemented.
- Mitigation effectiveness is verified.
Evidence: Brake hazard verification report BVR-09.
Rationale for grouping: Hazards are grouped by actuator path because that grouping matches the mitigation architecture.
examples.problem: The rationale is being used as proof. The test results should be cited as evidence and linked to the claim through clear sub-claims or reasoning.

guidelines.rationale: Rationale can explain local reasoning choices, but it cannot replace sub-claims, evidence, or a clear argument linking evidence to the claim. Treating rationale as support hides missing reasoning, missing evidence, or unsupported assumptions.
review_prompts: Is the rationale explaining a local choice, or trying to carry evidential weight?
If the rationale were removed, would the real support for the claim still remain?
guidelines.short_rule: Use rationale to explain a choice, never as the support that makes a claim true.
guidelines.statement: Use rationale, warrant, or justification text to explain why a wording, boundary, decomposition, or inference choice is acceptable; do not use it as the proof that a claim is true.
guidelines.title: Do not use rationale as hidden support

detection_hints: Look for justifications that cite test results or evidence rather than rationale.

repair.statement: Cite the artifact as evidence instead of asserting it in the rationale.
Add the sub-claims that connect that evidence to the claim.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the justification carries evidential weight that should sit in evidence or sub-claims.

examples.bad:
Claim: Sensor faults are adequately addressed.
Rationale: The item is intended for highway use.
examples.good:
Claim: Sensor faults are adequately addressed.
Scope: Applies to the highway operational design domain.
Local rationale: Sensor faults are grouped by detection mechanism because the mitigation set is organized along the same lines.
examples.problem: The rationale does not explain why this exact claim, breakdown, or reasoning step is acceptable; "intended for highway use" is scope information that belongs elsewhere and could be pasted onto many unrelated elements.

guidelines.rationale: Misaligned rationale creates false confidence and often reveals that the real concern is missing context, missing decomposition, missing evidence, or an unstated inference rule.
review_prompts: Does the rationale explain why this exact claim formulation, decomposition, or inference is acceptable?
Is it local, or is it trying to justify the whole branch?
Could the same text be pasted onto many different elements without change?
guidelines.short_rule: Keep each rationale local to the exact element or inference step it explains.
guidelines.statement: Any rationale, warrant, or justification shall address the exact claim, argument, or inference step to which it is attached and shall not explain a different issue elsewhere in the branch.
guidelines.title: Match each rationale to the element or inference it explains

detection_hints: Look for justifications that could be moved to other elements without losing meaning.

repair.statement: Rewrite the rationale so that it explains this exact element or inference step.
Move scope information out of the rationale into context.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the justification is local to its attached element.

examples.bad:
Claim: Detection timing is acceptable.
Linked solution: System validation report.
examples.good:
Claim: Detection timing is acceptable.
Sub-claim: Detection latency meets acceptance criterion AC-DET-07 for scenarios S1-S12.
Solution: System validation report SVR-04, section 6.3, table 12 (scenarios S1-S12).
examples.problem: The reviewer cannot tell which test, section, or lower-level argument is intended to show that detection timing is acceptable. The trace exists only in the author's head.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case without traceability cannot be effectively reviewed or maintained.
review_prompts: Can the reviewer identify the intended evidence path without having to infer it?
Is it clear which evidence path ultimately supports this claim?
Would two reviewers follow the same trace to the same evidence?
guidelines.short_rule: Give every claim a path to evidence, or mark it undeveloped deliberately.
guidelines.statement: Show, for each claim, the evidence path that supports it, either directly or through stated sub-claims and intermediate arguments.
guidelines.title: Make the evidence-support path explicit for every claim

detection_hints: Look for claims with no traceable path to evidence.
Look for solutions linked to claims without intermediate sub-claims when needed.

repair.statement: Attach the evidence element that supports the claim.
If no evidence is intended yet, mark the claim undeveloped deliberately rather than leaving the gap silent.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each claim has an explicit evidence path through sub-claims or direct solutions.

examples.bad:
Claim: Perception validation evidence is sufficient for this claim.
Evidence: Engineer working file WF-27.
examples.good:
Claim: Perception validation evidence is sufficient for this claim.
Evidence: Perception validation report PVR-08, rev B.
Evidence type: A validation report is an approved evidence type for this kind of claim.
Evidence basis: PVR-08 meets the defined criteria for that evidence type.
examples.problem: WF-27 is an engineer working file, not an approved evidence type for this claim. The reviewer cannot tell how to assess it.

guidelines.rationale: A reviewer should be able to recognize what kind of evidence is being used, what makes it acceptable for this purpose, and how it should be interpreted. If an artifact is not an approved evidence type, or does not meet the criteria required for that type, it becomes difficult to review consistently and easy to misuse in a safety argument.
review_prompts: Is the evidence type clearly defined?
Is the expected structure or content of the artifact defined?
Is it clear how the artifact is to be interpreted?
Is there a defined basis for reviewing, validating, or accepting this evidence type?
Could an independent reviewer examine the artifact consistently without relying on undocumented local knowledge?
guidelines.short_rule: Cite only artifacts whose evidence type is defined and whose criteria for that type are met.
guidelines.statement: Do not use evidence unless its artifact type is defined for safety case use and the artifact meets the criteria required for that type, so that it can be reviewed and assessed consistently.
guidelines.title: Use evidence types that can be independently reviewed

detection_hints: Look for evidence references to ad-hoc or working artifacts (working file, draft notes).

repair.statement: Cite an artifact whose evidence type is defined for this use, or state the criteria that make this artifact acceptable for that type.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the evidence type is defined and the artifact meets the type's criteria. Candidate when an ad-hoc artifact marker names the cited artifact.

examples.bad: TR-21 proves the braking controller is safe.
examples.good: Braking controller stopping distance meets acceptance criterion AC-BRK-04.
examples.problem: A test report supports a specific bounded property, not a whole safety conclusion; making the document the subject of the claim overreaches what the cited artifact can show.

guidelines.rationale: Evidence usually supports a specific fact or bounded property, not the whole safety conclusion by itself.
review_prompts: Is the goal naming a document instead of a supported property?
Is the evidential link too large for the cited artifact?
Would the claim remain meaningful if the artifact name changed?
guidelines.short_rule: Claim the fact the evidence establishes, not the document that holds it.
guidelines.statement: Write the claim as the fact or property being supported; do not make the goal say that a report, analysis, or test proves the safety conclusion.
guidelines.title: Claim the fact supported by the evidence, not the document

detection_hints: Look for claim text that names a report, document, or analysis as the subject.

repair.statement: Restate the claim as the fact the cited artifact establishes.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim subject is a property rather than a document. Candidate when an artifact noun is the subject of the claim, or an evidential verb makes an artifact the thing that proves the conclusion.

examples.bad: See validation report.
examples.good: See validation report VR-04, section 6.3, table 12, scenarios S14-S21.
examples.problem: A whole-report citation creates the appearance of support without making the evidential link easy to review; the reviewer cannot find the relevant material quickly.

guidelines.rationale: Broad references to whole reports create the illusion of support without making the evidential link easy to review.
review_prompts: Could a reviewer find the relevant support quickly?
Is the cited location precise enough?
Is the reference proportionate to the actual support being used?
guidelines.short_rule: Cite the exact section, table, figure, or test identifier, not a whole report.
guidelines.statement: Reference the exact section, figure, table, dataset, or artifact portion that supports the claim when practical.
guidelines.title: Cite precise evidence locations; avoid annex dumping

detection_hints: Look for evidence references that name an entire report without section/table/figure.

repair.statement: Add the section, table, figure, dataset, or test identifier that carries the support.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether evidence references are specific enough to be quickly verified. Candidate when an evidence reference names an artifact and carries no citation precision marker.

examples.bad:
Claim: Perception performance is acceptable.
Evidence: Perception validation report PVR-08.
examples.good:
Claim: Perception performance is acceptable for ODD-A daytime operation.
Evidence: Perception validation report PVR-08.
Context: Applies to software build SB-14 and sensor configuration C3.
Justification: Sufficiency is based on scenario coverage SC-21, acceptance thresholds AC-PER-04 to AC-PER-07, and the stated exclusion of dense fog conditions.
examples.problem: The report is cited, but the argument does not state what coverage, thresholds, configurations, or limitations make that report sufficient for this claim.

guidelines.rationale: A reviewer should not have to guess why a cited test, analysis, dataset, or review record is enough. The argument should make the sufficiency basis visible, such as relevant scope, configuration, scenario coverage, thresholds, acceptance conditions, and known limitations.
review_prompts: What makes this evidence enough for this claim?
Is the required scope, configuration, scenario set, or operating condition clear?
Is any threshold, pass criterion, or completeness expectation stated?
Are known limitations or uncovered conditions explicit?
Is the branch showing only that the evidence is relevant, or also that it is enough?
guidelines.short_rule: State what makes the cited evidence sufficient for this claim, not only relevant to it.
guidelines.statement: When a claim is supported by evidence, make clear what makes that evidence sufficient for that claim.
guidelines.title: Make the basis for evidence sufficiency explicit

detection_hints: Look for evidence cited without scope, threshold, or coverage justification.

repair.statement: State the coverage, thresholds, configuration, and limitations that make the evidence sufficient.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the basis for evidence sufficiency is explicit. Candidate when evidence is cited and no sufficiency basis marker appears in the branch.

examples.bad:
Claim: Detection timing meets acceptance criterion AC-DET-07.
Solution: Timing test report TR-18, section 5.2.
examples.good:
Claim: Detection timing meets acceptance criterion AC-DET-07.
Solution: Timing test report TR-18, section 5.2.
Inferential explanation: TR-18 shows measured detection latency below AC-DET-07 for scenarios S1-S12 in configuration C4. This supports the claim for that scenario set and configuration. Degraded sensor mode D3 is not covered and remains outside the supported scope.
examples.problem: The evidence is linked, but the reason it supports the claim is not explicitly documented anywhere reviewable; relevance, coverage, and limitations remain implicit.

guidelines.rationale: Evidence does not speak for itself. The safety case or linked assessment record must explain why the evidence bears on the claim.
review_prompts: Is it explicit why this evidence matters for this claim?
Is the inferential link documented in a reviewable form?
Does the documentation explain only support, or also limitations and possible refutation?
Has confirmation bias been considered?
guidelines.short_rule: Document why the cited evidence bears on this claim, including what it does not cover.
guidelines.statement: Ensure the inferential link between claim and evidence is explicitly documented and reviewable. The documentation shall explain how the cited evidence supports the claim, and where relevant how it reveals limitations or possible refutation.
guidelines.title: Explain how the evidence supports or refutes the claim

detection_hints: Look for evidence linked to claims without an accompanying inferential explanation.

repair.statement: Document why this evidence bears on this claim and what it does not cover.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the inferential link between claim and evidence is reviewable.

examples.bad: Evidence: Test summary on team wiki.
examples.good: Evidence: Test summary TSR-11, rev D, approved 2026-03-14, owner Safety Validation Team, stored in the controlled evidence repository.
examples.problem: The cited source has no fixed revision, no clear approval state, and no stable retrieval point for future review; the argument may silently lose validity if the page changes.

guidelines.rationale: Uncontrolled or mutable evidence is hard to verify, maintain, and re-assess. If a cited artifact can change after review, the argument may silently lose validity while still appearing supported.
review_prompts: Who owns the evidence?
Which version or revision is being cited?
Is the evidence retrieved from a controlled location?
Is the cited artifact fixed, or can it still change?
If it is a live document, is there an explicit mechanism that re-assesses affected claims when the document changes?
Is its status clear, for example draft, in review, approved, or released?
guidelines.short_rule: Keep evidence controlled: owner, version, date, status, and a stable retrieval location.
guidelines.statement: Evidence cited in the safety case should be under configuration or document control, with clear ownership, version or revision, date, status, and a stable retrieval location. Do not rely on mutable live documents as evidence unless the cited version is fixed or the change process explicitly triggers re-assessment of the affected claim.
guidelines.title: Keep evidence controlled: owner, version, date, status, repository

detection_hints: Look for evidence references with no version, date, owner, or controlled location.

repair.statement: Add owner, version or revision, date, status, and a controlled retrieval location to the reference.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each evidence reference includes owner, version, date, status, and stable location (directly or via linked control mechanism). Candidate when none of the control attribute markers is present; the result names which are missing.

examples.bad: See braking verification page in Confluence.
examples.good:
See Braking Verification Plan BVP-04, rev C, approved 2026-03-11.

Or, equivalently: See archived snapshot of Confluence page CP-118, version 17, captured 2026-03-11.
examples.problem: The cited page is mutable; future reviewers cannot retrieve the same content that was originally reviewed, which breaks reproducibility and configuration control.

guidelines.rationale: This rule is the specific citation case of EV.7. If cited evidence can change after review, the safety case may appear supported while its actual evidential basis has changed or disappeared. This breaks reproducibility, reviewability, and configuration control.
review_prompts: Could this cited content change without the safety case being updated?
Is the cited state fixed, versioned, or archived?
Can a future reviewer retrieve the exact same content that was reviewed?
If the source is live, is there an explicit process that triggers re-assessment of affected claims when it changes?
guidelines.short_rule: Cite a fixed, versioned, or archived state, never live mutable content.
guidelines.statement: Do not cite live mutable content as evidence unless the cited state is fixed, versioned, archived, or otherwise controlled so that the reviewed argument always refers to the same content.
guidelines.title: Cite fixed evidence, not live mutable content

detection_hints: Look for citations to wikis, live shared docs, or other mutable URLs without a fixed version or snapshot.

repair.statement: Cite a fixed revision, version, or archived snapshot rather than live content.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the cited content state is fixed, versioned, or archived. Candidate when a mutable source marker is present and no fixing marker accompanies it.

examples.bad:
Claim: Unsafe torque requests are prevented during degraded localization.
The safety case includes a free-text explanation of the controller behavior, but the relevant design basis is not identified through context and no supporting artifacts are linked.
examples.good:
Claim: Unsafe torque requests are prevented during degraded localization.
Design basis: Braking control design specification BCS-02, degraded-mode requirements DMR-04, and interface definition IFD-07.
Evidence: Verification report VFR-11 shows that the specified behavior is implemented and verified.
examples.problem: The claim relies on undocumented system knowledge instead of controlled artifacts.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case should argue from reviewable evidence, not from what engineers happen to know. When system knowledge is written directly into the safety case without a supporting source, the argument becomes hard to verify, hard to maintain, and difficult to assess for completeness. It also becomes unclear whether the claim is supported by an approved design basis or only by current team understanding.
review_prompts: Is this claim supported by controlled documentation or other identified evidence?
Is the safety case describing how the system works instead of arguing from documented sources?
Would the claim still be supportable if the original engineer were unavailable?
Should this material be moved to a specification, design description, interface definition, hazard analysis, or other work product and then cited as evidence?
guidelines.short_rule: Argue from cited documentation, not from undocumented engineering knowledge.
guidelines.statement: Do not support claims by relying on undocumented engineering knowledge, design understanding, or verbal explanation. Claims about system behavior, design, interfaces, mitigations, or operating limits should be grounded in controlled documentation or other identified evidence.
guidelines.title: Do not argue directly from undocumented system knowledge

detection_hints: Look for free-text design explanations in the safety case without linked specification or evidence.

repair.statement: Cite the design basis as evidence rather than describing system behaviour in the argument.
Identify the specification or interface definition as context.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the argument relies on undocumented system knowledge rather than cited artifacts.

examples.bad:
Claim: Hazard analysis is complete for the defined ODD.
Evidence: Hazard analysis report HAR-03.
examples.good:
Claim: Hazard analysis is complete for the defined ODD.
Evidence: Hazard analysis report HAR-03.
Challenge: The analysis may not cover scenarios introduced after the most recent ODD revision.
Response: Change-impact review CIR-12 confirms newly added scenarios were re-examined.
Challenge: The chosen method has known coverage limits for emergent multi-actor interactions.
Response: Supplementary scenario-based analysis SBA-04 addresses that gap.
examples.problem: A reviewer could reasonably ask whether the analysis covered scenarios introduced after the most recent ODD revision, whether the chosen method has known coverage limits for emergent multi-actor interactions, and whether the ODD assumptions still hold. None of these challenges are visible in the argument.

guidelines.rationale: A credible safety case should not only present supporting material. It should also make important doubts visible and show how they are handled. This fits well with GSN-style review, where challenge is used to test whether a claim, inference, or supporting material still stands when subjected to scrutiny.
review_prompts: What could invalidate this claim or reasoning step?
What assumptions, confounders, uncertainties, or biases are relevant here?
Could this evidence be incomplete, misleading, or outside the supported scope?
Is the challenge really against the claim, the reasoning, the evidence, an assumption, or the stated scope?
Are important doubts visible in the argument, or left unstated?
guidelines.short_rule: Make plausible challenges to the claim, reasoning, or evidence visible, and address them.
guidelines.statement: Where a reviewer could reasonably question whether a claim, reasoning step, evidence item, assumption, or stated scope is valid, complete, applicable, or sufficiently reliable, make that challenge explicit and address it where needed.
guidelines.title: Identify and address plausible challenges to claims, reasoning, and evidence

detection_hints: Look for branches presenting only supporting material with no challenges or responses.

repair.statement: Raise the plausible challenge as an explicit challenge element and resolve it.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether plausible reviewer challenges to the claim, reasoning, or evidence are visible and addressed.

examples.bad:
Claim: Localization accuracy is acceptable within the defined ODD.
Hidden assumption (not stated): Map data used at runtime is current.
examples.good:
Claim: Localization accuracy is acceptable within the defined ODD.
Assumption: Map data used at runtime is no more than 7 days out of date.
Justification: Map update process MAP-PROC-02 enforces a 7-day refresh cycle and is monitored by KPI MAP-KPI-01.
Re-assessment trigger: Sustained KPI breach or change to the map update process.
examples.problem: A reviewer cannot judge whether the assumption is reasonable, whether it is monitored, or what would invalidate it. If the assumption fails, the affected claim may silently lose support.

guidelines.rationale: Unstated or weakly founded assumptions are a common cause of later argument invalidation. That aligns well with UL 4600’s treatment of assumptions and lifecycle monitoring. GSN also treats assumptions as a distinct element type, so checking whether something is really an assumption is appropriate.
review_prompts: What must be true for this branch to hold?
Why is this assumption reasonable, and how would we know if it became false?
Is this really an assumption, or should it instead be represented as context, a claim, or evidence?
guidelines.short_rule: State assumptions explicitly, justify why each is reasonable, and monitor them where needed.
guidelines.statement: Do not rely on hidden assumptions. State assumptions explicitly, explain why they are reasonable, and ensure they are monitored or otherwise controlled where needed.
guidelines.title: Make assumptions explicit and justify why they are reasonable

detection_hints: Look for branches whose validity depends on a condition that is not stated as an assumption or context.

repair.statement: State the hidden condition explicitly as an assumption.
Justify why the assumption is reasonable and how it is monitored.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether implicit assumptions are made explicit, justified, and monitorable.

examples.bad:
Claim: Residual risk is acceptable.
Evidence: Safety review board statement that residual risk is considered acceptable.
examples.good:
Claim: Residual risk is acceptable.
Evidence:
- Quantitative risk analysis QRA-09 showing residual risk below the defined threshold.
- Operational data summary ODS-03 covering 18 months of comparable exposure with no injury-class events.
Expert review: Safety review board record SRB-2026-04 confirming the analysis method, inputs, and conclusion are consistent with established practice.
Note: Expert review is corroborating, not substituting for, the underlying analysis and data.
examples.problem: Expert judgment is being used as the sole basis for the claim, with no analysis, data, or independent corroboration that a reviewer can examine.

guidelines.rationale: Expert opinion may be useful, but unsupported opinion is weak support and can easily outstate what is actually known.
review_prompts: Is the opinion supported by data, literature, documented analysis, or another explicit technical basis?
Is the context of applicability clear and argued?
If the opinion remains weakly supported, is lifecycle monitoring in place where needed?
guidelines.short_rule: Do not rest a claim on expert judgment alone; state its basis and corroborate it.
guidelines.statement: Do not rely on expert judgment alone unless its basis, limits, and corroborating support are stated, or the residual uncertainty is monitored over the lifecycle where appropriate.
guidelines.title: Do not rely on uncorroborated expert judgment alone

detection_hints: Look for evidence consisting only of expert statements without supporting analysis or data.

repair.statement: Add the analysis or data that corroborates the judgment.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether expert judgment is corroborated by data, analysis, or lifecycle monitoring. Candidate when an uncorroborated judgment marker carries the support with no analysis or data cited alongside it.

examples.bad:
Claim: Unexpected roadside object class X is sufficiently rare that residual risk is acceptable.
Evidence: Design-time analysis suggesting object class X is rare.
Justification: The design-time rarity assumption is treated as fully proven; no operational follow-up is defined.
examples.good:
Claim: Unexpected roadside object class X is sufficiently rare that residual risk is acceptable.
Acknowledged uncertainty: The rarity assumption is not fully confirmed at design time.
Field monitoring: Occurrence of roadside object class X is monitored in operation.
Reassessment trigger: Observed frequency or associated incidents exceed threshold T.
examples.problem: The available data does not fully establish the operational frequency of object class X, but the remaining uncertainty is not made explicit and no lifecycle monitoring is defined to confirm or challenge the claim during operation.

guidelines.rationale: Some claims depend partly on assumptions, limited evidence, or expected field behavior. In such cases, the safety case should not hide the remaining uncertainty. It should explain it and define how operation will provide feedback.
review_prompts: What part of this claim is not fully supported at design time?
Can that remaining uncertainty only be reduced through operational or field data?
Is lifecycle monitoring defined for that uncertainty?
Are reassessment triggers identified?
guidelines.short_rule: Where design-time support is partial, say so and define monitoring and re-assessment triggers.
guidelines.statement: When a claim cannot be fully supported at design time, make the remaining uncertainty explicit and define lifecycle monitoring that can confirm or challenge the claim during operation.
guidelines.title: Monitor claims that cannot be fully supported at design time

detection_hints: Look for claims with partial design-time support and no defined lifecycle monitoring.

repair.statement: State the unconfirmed condition as an assumption with a re-assessment trigger.
Narrow the claim to what design-time evidence actually supports.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether claims with residual design-time uncertainty have defined monitoring and reassessment triggers.

examples.bad: This camera is proven in use and is therefore acceptable for autonomous truck operation.
examples.good:
Claim: Reuse of camera safety credit is justified for the current application.
Context:
- Original application: conventional passenger vehicle ADAS use.
- Current application: autonomous heavy truck operation.
Justification: Safety credit may only be reused if the original and current contexts are shown to be sufficiently comparable in the aspects that matter to safety.
Sub-claims:
- The original and current operating environments are sufficiently comparable.
- The original and current duty cycles are sufficiently comparable.
- The original and current interfaces and installation conditions are sufficiently comparable.
- The original and current safety roles and failure consequences are sufficiently comparable.
- Any non-comparable differences are addressed by additional evidence or explicit limitations.
examples.problem: The claim takes safety credit from another context (passenger vehicle ADAS use) without showing that the original application, operating conditions, interfaces, and safety role are sufficiently comparable to autonomous heavy truck operation.

guidelines.rationale: Safety confidence gained in one context does not automatically remain valid in another. Differences in operating environment, purpose, interfaces, duty cycle, autonomy role, or assumptions can invalidate the reuse.
review_prompts: What safety confidence, evidence, or assessment result is being reused from another context?
Is the original operating context sufficiently comparable to the current one?
Have differences in purpose, environment, interfaces, or assumptions been identified?
Have the limitations of the original assessment been stated?
guidelines.short_rule: Show that reused safety credit came from a sufficiently comparable context.
guidelines.statement: Do not rely on safety credit from proven-in-use technology, legacy technology, COTS, prior assessments, standard conformance, or prior practice unless you show that the original context is sufficiently comparable to the current one.
guidelines.title: Do not reuse safety credit from another context without showing it still applies

detection_hints: Look for proven-in-use or legacy claims with no comparability argument.

repair.statement: Argue comparability of the original and current context as sub-claims.
State the basis on which the reused credit is held to apply.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether reused safety credit is supported by an explicit comparability argument. Candidate when a reuse marker appears and no comparability argument accompanies it.

examples.bad:
Claim: Residual risk from unexpected roadside object encounters is acceptable in operation.
Support: field incident history and operational monitoring.
Note: Three roadside-object anomalies were reported, but none caused injury and none could be reproduced, so they are not safety-relevant.
examples.good:
Claim: Residual risk from unexpected roadside object encounters is acceptable in operation.
Support: field incident history and operational monitoring.
Treatment: The three anomalies are recorded, grouped, and evaluated as negative field feedback. The argument explains whether they challenge the rarity assumption, whether they show a gap in object coverage, and whether more analysis or mitigation is needed.
examples.problem: The argument uses operational feedback but dismisses adverse signals simply because they were non-injury and non-reproducible; together they may indicate the rarity assumption is less reliable than it appears.

guidelines.rationale: Operational feedback is often used to support claims about residual risk, rarity, adequacy of existing controls, or continued acceptability in service. In those branches, non-injury or non-reproducibility does not make a signal irrelevant. Several weak signals together may show that the argument is less reliable than it appears.
review_prompts: Is this branch relying on operational experience or field feedback as part of its support?
Are incidents defined broadly enough to include near misses, close calls, and anomalies that could have led to harm?
Is adverse operational feedback being screened out too aggressively?
Is the argument considering the combined signal from multiple incidents or anomalies?
Is adverse operational evidence explicitly recorded, evaluated, and addressed?
guidelines.short_rule: Do not dismiss field anomalies because they caused no injury or could not be reproduced.
guidelines.statement: When a claim relies on operational experience, field monitoring, incident history, or proven-in-use style reasoning, do not dismiss incidents, near misses, anomalies, or failure reports merely because they have not recurred, cannot yet be reproduced, or did not lead to harm.
guidelines.title: Do not dismiss operational feedback because it is non-reproducible or non-injury

detection_hints: Look for arguments that use operational data and discount non-injury or non-reproducible incidents.

repair.statement: Record and evaluate the adverse operational feedback rather than dismissing it.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether adverse operational feedback is recorded, grouped, and evaluated rather than silently dismissed. Candidate when a dismissal marker appears in a branch that relies on operational experience.

examples.bad:
Claim: Collision risk with cut-in vehicles is low.
Evidence: Simulation results SIM-12.
Justification: No collisions were observed in the simulation results, therefore the risk is low.
examples.good:
Claim: Collision risk with cut-in vehicles is acceptably low.
Evidence:
- Simulation results SIM-12.
- Track test report TR-08.
- Field incident review FR-03.
Argument: Why SIM-12 is valid for this hazard and what scenario space it covers; what limitations remain in the simulation model; how TR-08 corroborates important behaviors in representative test conditions; how FR-03 is used to check whether operational experience challenges the claim.
examples.problem: The branch treats simulation results alone as sufficient proof that risk is low, without showing that the simulation is valid for this claim, that the modeled scenarios are adequate, or that important model limitations are understood.

guidelines.rationale: Operational exposure can miss catastrophic but rare outcomes. Simulation can miss modeling defects and abstraction errors.
review_prompts: Is simulation alone being treated as enough to show low risk?
Is operational history alone being treated as enough to show low risk?
Has simulation validity for this claim not been shown?
Are corroborating evidence, scenario limits, or model limitations missing?
guidelines.short_rule: Do not infer low risk from uneventful operation or unvalidated simulation alone.
guidelines.statement: Do not infer low risk for a known hazard solely from uneventful operational history or from simulation whose credibility for the claim has not been demonstrated.
guidelines.title: Do not argue low risk from operational experience or unvalidated simulation alone

detection_hints: Look for low-risk claims supported only by simulation or only by uneventful operational time.

repair.statement: Add corroborating evidence of a different type.
Argue why the simulation or operational basis is valid for this claim.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether low-risk claims combine multiple corroborating evidence types and address simulation validity.

examples.bad:
Claim: Planning failure modes are adequately covered by the test set.
Evidence: Scenario Selection Report SSR-04.
Justification: The scenario set is based on human-driven fleet data and therefore covers relevant road situations.
examples.good:
Claim: Planning failure modes are adequately covered by the test set.
Evidence:
- Scenario Selection Report SSR-04.
- Planner Failure Analysis Report PFA-03.
- Edge Case Test Specification ETS-07.
Justification: Coverage is based not only on human-driven scenarios, but also on autonomy-specific planner failure analysis and identified edge cases.
examples.problem: The branch assumes that human-driven data is enough to cover planning failures, but the autonomous planner may enter unusual states or produce behaviors that human drivers would not normally create.

guidelines.rationale: Autonomous systems can encounter operating situations and failure combinations that are uncommon in human driving. Human-derived data and human-designed tests may therefore miss important autonomy-specific risks.
review_prompts: Is the claim supported mainly by human-operated data or human-designed tests?
Could the autonomous system encounter situations or create hazards that are uncommon in human driving?
Are autonomy-specific failure modes and edge cases explicitly considered?
Is there evidence that the test basis covers autonomy-specific failures, not only human-driving situations?
guidelines.short_rule: Do not assume human-derived data or human-designed tests cover autonomy-specific failures.
guidelines.statement: Do not assume that human-operated data sets or human-designed test plans are sufficient to cover autonomy-specific failures or edge cases.
guidelines.title: Do not assume human data or human-designed tests cover autonomy-specific failures

detection_hints: Look for claims about autonomy coverage backed only by human-driven datasets or human-designed scenarios.

repair.statement: Add evidence covering autonomy-specific failure modes and edge cases.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the test basis covers autonomy-specific failure modes and edge cases.

examples.bad: Claim: Localization integrity is sufficient for safe fallback.
examples.good:
Claim: Localization integrity is sufficient for safe fallback.
Assumption: Localization integrity remains within bound L1 during fallback maneuver.

Or, if that dependency should be argued rather than assumed:

Claim: Localization integrity is sufficient for safe fallback.
Sub-claim: Localization integrity remains within bound L1 during fallback maneuver.
Evidence: Fallback localization analysis report FLA-03.
examples.problem: The branch depends on an unstated condition about localization performance during fallback (that integrity remains within bound L1), but that dependency is only implicit and a reviewer cannot see what must hold for the claim to be valid.

guidelines.rationale: Hidden dependencies are a common reason for late argument invalidation. Making them visible helps the reviewer see what the branch depends on and decide whether that dependency should remain an assumption, be stated as context, or be argued as a claim.
review_prompts: What must be true for this claim or strategy to hold, but is not currently stated?
Is the hidden dependency local to the claim, or to the reasoning step?
Should this dependency be represented as an assumption, as context, or as a claim that must be proved?
guidelines.short_rule: State a dependency where it constrains the argument, as an assumption, context, or claim.
guidelines.statement: When a claim or reasoning step depends on something that is not currently stated, make that dependency explicit at the point where it constrains the argument, using an assumption, context element, or subclaim as appropriate.
guidelines.title: Document unstated assumptions at the point of use

detection_hints: Look for claims whose validity depends on conditions not stated as assumption, context, or subclaim.

repair.statement: State the unstated dependency as an assumption at the point where it constrains the argument.
If the dependency must be shown rather than assumed, add it as a sub-claim.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether unstated dependencies are made visible at the point of use.

examples.bad:
Claim: Traffic signal interpretation is sufficiently reliable for safe intersection handling.
Assumption: Infrastructure behaves correctly.
examples.good:
Claim: Traffic signal interpretation is sufficiently reliable for safe intersection handling.
Assumption: Within the defined ODD, traffic signals managed by the identified road authorities are assumed to conform to the referenced control standard.
Monitoring: Violations are tracked through field feedback and incident analysis.

Or, if several dependencies are involved, split into multiple assumptions:
- Traffic signal installations in the defined ODD conform to the referenced control standard.
- Detected traffic signal anomalies are captured through field feedback.
examples.problem: The assumption is too broad; it does not identify which infrastructure, which behaviors, which authorities, or what kinds of failure are being assumed away, so it cannot be checked, challenged, or monitored.

guidelines.rationale: Over-broad assumptions can make a claim appear closed while removing most of its review value. If an argument depends on an assumption, the assumption should be narrow enough to understand, evaluate, and monitor where needed.
review_prompts: Is the assumption matched to the scope of the claim it constrains?
Can the assumption be checked, challenged, or monitored?
Does the assumption hide several different dependencies that should be separated?
Would the branch become clearer if the assumption were narrowed or split?
guidelines.short_rule: Keep each assumption narrow, specific, and monitorable, and split ones that bundle dependencies.
guidelines.statement: Do not use assumptions that are broader than the claim scope or so vague that they cannot be checked, challenged, or monitored.
guidelines.title: Keep assumptions bounded, specific, and monitorable

detection_hints: Look for assumptions that are vague, universal, or unmonitorable.

repair.statement: Split an assumption that bundles several dependencies into one assumption each.
Narrow the assumption to something that can be checked, challenged, or monitored.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each assumption is narrow, specific, and monitorable where needed. Candidate when an unbounded assumption marker appears with no stated scope, threshold, or monitoring.

examples.bad:
Initial branch:
Claim: Fallback behavior is acceptably safe.
Reviewer challenge raised informally: What if localization drops out during fallback?
The challenge is not promoted into the safety case and remains in review notes only.
examples.good:
Make the challenge explicit:
Challenge: Fallback behavior may not be acceptably safe if localization drops out during fallback.
Representation: In GSN this may be shown as a Counter Claim; in CAE this may be shown as a defeater.
Status: Undeveloped (while analysis is ongoing).

Possible resolutions:
- Challenge rejected: Add evidence (Fallback localization analysis FLA-04, Fallback test report FTR-09); claim retained.
- Challenge sustained: Narrow the claim to "Fallback behavior is acceptably safe under conditions with validated localization continuity."
- Challenge partly sustained: Add dependency "Localization continuity is maintained during fallback" plus monitoring of continuity violations.
- Not yet resolved: Open Issue "Impact of localization dropout during fallback remains unresolved and requires additional analysis."
examples.problem: A plausible reviewer challenge has been left in review comments and reviewer intuition rather than made explicit in the safety case, so it cannot be tracked, resolved, or shown as an open issue.

guidelines.rationale: A credible safety case should not leave plausible challenges only in review comments or reviewer intuition. Good reviews expose weaknesses early. Making the challenge explicit helps ensure that it is either resolved properly or left visible until it is resolved.
review_prompts: What exactly is the reviewer challenge?
Should this challenge be made explicit as a Counter Claim, defeater, or other challenge element?
Has the challenge been rejected, sustained, or left unresolved?
If sustained, has the original branch been updated appropriately?
If unresolved, is the open issue visible and traceable?
guidelines.short_rule: Raise a plausible reviewer challenge as an explicit element and resolve it visibly.
guidelines.statement: When review raises a plausible What if X? challenge, make that challenge explicit and resolve it visibly in the safety case. Depending on the method, this may be represented as a GSN Counter Claim, a CAE defeater, or another explicit challenge element. The resolution may reject the challenge, narrow or revise the original claim, add supporting evidence, introduce assumptions and monitoring, or leave a visible open issue if the matter is not yet resolved.
guidelines.title: Make plausible reviewer challenges explicit and resolve them

detection_hints: Look for plausible reviewer challenges that have not been promoted into the safety case.

repair.statement: Raise the reviewer challenge as a counter claim or defeater in the argument.
If the challenge is sustained, narrow the claim to what still holds.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether plausible reviewer challenges are made explicit and visibly resolved.

examples.bad: The system is acceptably safe because the safety case shows acceptable safety.
examples.good: The system is acceptably safe because hazards H1-H12 are mitigated by controls C1-C8, and the controls are verified by reports VR-01 to VR-08 against acceptance criteria AC-01 to AC-12.
examples.problem: The support restates the claim using different words; it provides no independent grounds for the conclusion.

guidelines.rationale: Circular support creates the appearance of argument without adding any new support.
review_prompts: Would the support still work if the parent claim were not assumed true?
Is the same conclusion being repeated with different words?
guidelines.short_rule: Support a claim with independent grounds, never by restating or renaming it.
guidelines.statement: Do not support a claim by restating it, renaming it, or assuming it in the support.
guidelines.title: Avoid circular reasoning

detection_hints: Look for support that restates or renames the parent claim.

repair.statement: Replace the restatement with support that does not assume the claim.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether support adds independent reasoning or merely restates the claim.

examples.bad:
Claim: Brake fault handling is acceptable.
Evidence: Brake fault handling requirements are documented.
examples.good:
Claim: Brake fault handling is acceptable.
Sub-claims:
- Brake fault handling requirements are correctly defined.
- Implemented brake fault handling satisfies the defined requirements.
Evidence:
- Brake fault handling requirements specification BRS-04.
- Brake fault handling verification report BVR-09.
examples.problem: Documented requirements may be necessary, but they do not by themselves show that brake fault handling is acceptable; the inferential link between requirements existing and acceptable fault handling is missing.

guidelines.rationale: A common defect is to attach true or relevant material to the wrong claim, so the branch appears supported even though the actual inference is missing.
review_prompts: Does this evidence support this exact claim?
Is the evidence only relevant to a different or neighboring claim?
Is the missing support actually a different intermediate claim that has not been stated?
guidelines.short_rule: Attach evidence to the exact claim it supports, not to a neighbouring one.
guidelines.statement: Do not use evidence or supporting statements that may be true but do not support the immediate claim being made.
guidelines.title: Avoid irrelevant premises

detection_hints: Look for evidence whose actual scope supports a different claim than the one it is attached to.

repair.statement: Add the intermediate claim that the cited evidence actually supports.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each evidence item supports the immediate claim it is attached to.

examples.bad:
Claim: No other credible hazards exist.
Evidence: HARA report HAR-03.
Justification: The HARA identified all relevant hazards, and no further hazards were found.
examples.good:
Claim: Hazard identification is sufficiently complete for the defined scope.
Context: Applies to the defined item, ODD, and lifecycle scope.
Evidence:
- HARA report HAR-03.
- STPA report STP-02.
- Hazard review record HRR-07.
Justification: Complementary hazard identification methods and review coverage have been applied for the defined scope.
examples.problem: The branch treats absence of newly discovered hazards as proof that no other credible hazards exist, rather than as a bounded completeness claim about the search.

guidelines.rationale: Not finding a problem is not the same as showing that the problem does not exist. Claims about completeness or absence need support from the search basis, scope, and adequacy of the methods used.
review_prompts: Is not found being treated as does not exist?
Is the claim really about completeness of the search, rather than absolute absence?
Was the search for contrary evidence demonstrably adequate for the stated scope?
guidelines.short_rule: Do not argue from absence: nothing found is not evidence that nothing exists.
guidelines.statement: Do not treat lack of discovered evidence against a claim as positive evidence for the claim.
guidelines.title: Avoid arguing from ignorance

detection_hints: Look for completeness or absence claims justified only by absence-of-finding.

repair.statement: Restate the claim as a bounded completeness claim about the search that was performed.
Cite the search basis, methods, and coverage as evidence.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether absence-based claims are reframed as bounded completeness claims with adequate search coverage. Candidate when an absence phrase carries the support for a completeness claim.

examples.bad:
Claim: The autonomous vehicle is safer than a human driver.
Evidence: Simulation report SIM-09.
Justification: The autonomous vehicle had fewer simulated collisions than the human-driver baseline.
examples.good:
Claim: For the defined ODD and stated comparison metric, the autonomous vehicle has lower collision rate than the specified human-driver baseline.
Context: Comparison applies to ODD-A, metric M1, and baseline definition BD-02.
Evidence:
- Simulation report SIM-09.
- Baseline comparison report BCR-03.
- Scenario validity report SVR-04.
Justification: The compared cases use matched scope, scenarios, metrics, and confidence basis.
examples.problem: The comparison may be unjustified if the simulation conditions, scenario coverage, driver model, metrics, and confidence are not shown to be appropriate and comparable.

guidelines.rationale: Comparison-based arguments can look persuasive while hiding differences in scope, operating conditions, metrics, evidence quality, or confidence. Distinctions can also be misused to dismiss relevant comparators without showing why the difference matters.
review_prompts: What exactly is being compared or distinguished?
Is the basis of comparison or distinction explicit?
Are the compared cases matched in scope, operating conditions, metrics, and confidence level?
If a difference is claimed, is it shown why that difference matters to the argument?
