guidelines.short_rule: State the basis of any comparison or distinction, and show the cases are matched.
guidelines.statement: Do not claim that one case is equivalent to, safer than, better than, or different from another unless the basis of comparison or distinction is explicit and relevant to the claim being made.
guidelines.title: Avoid unjustified comparison or unjustified distinction

detection_hints: Look for safer-than or different-from claims without an explicit basis of comparison.

repair.statement: State the basis of comparison as context on the claim.
Argue why the compared cases are matched in scope, metric, and confidence.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether comparisons or distinctions are matched in scope, conditions, metrics, and confidence. Candidate when a comparison marker appears and no basis of comparison is stated in context or justification.

examples.bad:
Claim: The item is acceptably safe across the defined ODD.
Evidence: Road test report RTR-05 covering 12 daylight highway runs in dry conditions.
Justification: No safety-critical events were observed during testing.
examples.good:
Either narrow the claim:
Claim: The item is acceptably safe for the tested daytime highway subset of the ODD.
Context: Applies only to dry daytime highway operation under the conditions covered in RTR-05.
Evidence: Road test report RTR-05.

Or expand the evidence to match the broader claim:
Claim: The item is acceptably safe across the defined ODD.
Evidence:
- Road test report RTR-05.
- Night and weather test report NWT-03.
- Scenario coverage analysis SCA-04.
- Edge-case test report ETR-02.
Justification: The combined evidence set provides coverage across the claimed ODD, including relevant distributions and edge cases.
examples.problem: The claim covers the full ODD, but the evidence covers only a small and narrow subset of operating conditions; the sample is too limited in size and representativeness to support the broader claim.

guidelines.rationale: A small or skewed data set can support only a correspondingly narrow claim.
review_prompts: Is the sample size adequate for the confidence implied?
Does the data distribution match the ODD and edge cases?
Is the claim broader than the sample supports?
guidelines.short_rule: Keep the claim no broader than the sample size and representativeness support.
guidelines.statement: Do not generalize too far from too little data, or from data that does not match the operating context being claimed.
guidelines.title: Avoid sample-size and representativeness fallacies

detection_hints: Look for broad claims supported by narrow or small data sets.

repair.statement: Narrow the claim to the conditions the sample actually covers.
Or extend the evidence set to cover the breadth the claim states.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether sample size and representativeness match the breadth of the claim.

examples.bad:
Claim: Residual collision risk is 3.742 x 10^-7 per hour.
Evidence: Quantitative risk analysis report QRA-05.
examples.good:
Claim: Residual collision risk is below the accepted threshold for the defined operating conditions.
Context: Applies under the assumptions and scenario scope defined in QRA-05.
Evidence: Quantitative risk analysis report QRA-05.
Justification: The result is reported with precision consistent with model uncertainty and stated confidence.

Or, where a numeric claim is still appropriate:
Claim: Residual collision risk is estimated to be on the order of 10^-7 per hour for the defined operating conditions.
Context: Estimate is subject to the assumptions, uncertainty, and confidence limits stated in QRA-05.
Evidence: Quantitative risk analysis report QRA-05.
examples.problem: The stated value suggests a level of certainty that may not be justified by the model assumptions, input data quality, scenario coverage, or confidence bounds.

guidelines.rationale: A highly precise number can give a false impression of certainty. When uncertainty, confidence, model limits, or input assumptions are weak, the stated precision should reflect that.
review_prompts: Does the number imply a level of certainty the method cannot support?
Are uncertainty, assumptions, and confidence bounds stated where needed?
Is the stated precision greater than the quality of the underlying evidence or model?
Would a rounded value or bounded statement better reflect the real knowledge state?
guidelines.short_rule: State numbers only to the precision the model, data, and assumptions justify.
guidelines.statement: Do not present numerical precision beyond what the evidence, model, assumptions, or method can justify.
guidelines.title: Avoid pseudo-precision

detection_hints: Look for many-significant-digit numerical claims without uncertainty or confidence statement.

repair.statement: State the figure to the precision the method supports, with its uncertainty or confidence bound.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether numerical precision is consistent with model and data uncertainty. Candidate when a figure carries more significant digits than the published threshold and no uncertainty marker accompanies it.

thresholds.note: A risk or performance figure stated to more significant digits than this, with no stated uncertainty, is a candidate signal.

examples.bad:
Claim: Sensor robustness is acceptable.
Evidence: Sensor performance test report SPR-08.
Justification: The reported test results show robust detection performance.
examples.good:
Claim: Sensor robustness is acceptable for the defined conditions.
Evidence:
- Sensor performance test report SPR-08.
- Obscuration test report OTR-03.
- Environmental degradation test report EDR-05.
Justification: The argument addresses both supporting and limiting evidence for the claimed operating conditions.

Or, if contrary evidence exists, scope it:
Claim: Sensor robustness is acceptable for the defined conditions.
Evidence:
- Sensor performance test report SPR-08.
- Environmental degradation anomaly review EAR-02.
Context: Claim excludes heavy mud obscuration beyond the tested condition range.
Justification: Known degradation limits are explicitly addressed and reflected in the claim scope.
examples.problem: The branch cites supportive performance results but omits known obscuration, contamination, or environmental degradation evidence that a reviewer would naturally expect for a robustness claim.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case becomes misleading when it presents only supporting material and leaves out evidence that could weaken, limit, or challenge the claim.
review_prompts: What evidence would a critical reviewer reasonably expect to see for this claim?
Is any known anomaly, failure, exclusion, or limitation being left unaddressed?
Does the omitted material affect the meaning, scope, or credibility of the claim?
Is contrary evidence explicitly addressed rather than silently ignored?
guidelines.short_rule: Include the evidence a critical reviewer expects, and answer known contrary evidence.
guidelines.statement: Do not omit evidence that a skeptical reviewer would naturally expect, and do not leave known contrary evidence unanswered.
guidelines.title: Avoid omission of key evidence and ignoring counter-evidence

detection_hints: Look for branches that present only supporting evidence with no acknowledgement of known limits or contrary evidence.

repair.statement: Add the evidence a critical reviewer would expect, including contrary evidence.
Or narrow the claim so that the omitted conditions are outside its scope.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether known limiting or contrary evidence is addressed or scoped out.

examples.bad: The braking controller is safe in automated mode with valid localization because tests passed.
examples.good:
Claim: Braking controller safety is acceptable.
Scope: Applies in automated mode.
Dependency: Valid localization is available.
Evidence: Brake controller verification report BVR-09.
Reasoning: The cited verification evidence is relevant to the defined operating conditions.
examples.problem: The sentence mixes claim, context, assumption, and evidential reasoning in one statement; the reader must infer the role of each part.

guidelines.rationale: Review becomes harder when the reader must infer the role of a statement. Clear signposting reduces confusion between argument elements and makes the structure easier to inspect.
review_prompts: Is the reader forced to infer the role of the statement?
Are claims, context, assumptions, and justifications mixed together?
Is evidence clearly identifiable as evidence rather than explanation or claim text?
guidelines.short_rule: Signpost each element's role in its wording so no reader has to guess what it does.
guidelines.statement: Make it clear whether a statement is functioning as a claim, evidence reference, context, assumption, or justification.
guidelines.title: Use explicit signposting of argument element roles

detection_hints: Look for prose statements that mix claim, context, assumption, and evidence in one sentence.

repair.statement: Split the statement so that each part sits in the element whose role it plays.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each statement is clearly signposted with its argument element role. Candidate when an inference connective appears inside claim text, which signals reasoning that the structure should carry.

examples.bad: The item is safe.
examples.good: The item is acceptably safe for daytime urban operation in ODD-A under assumptions A1-A4, with open issue OI-03 for night rain behavior.
examples.problem: The claim has no operating scope and uses absolute confidence language; it overstates closure and hides any unresolved uncertainty.

guidelines.rationale: Safety cases should communicate justified confidence, not absolute assurance when support is partial, bounded, or still open in some respects.
review_prompts: Is the scope of the claim explicit?
Is unresolved uncertainty visible?
Does the wording overstate closure?
Does the confidence language match the actual support?
guidelines.short_rule: State the operating scope, and match confidence language to the actual support.
guidelines.statement: State the operating scope and use confidence language that reflects the actual support and any open issues.
guidelines.title: Use scoped claims and qualified confidence language

detection_hints: Look for unscoped claims using absolute confidence language (is safe, is correct).

repair.statement: State the operating scope and match the confidence wording to the actual support.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether claims state operating scope and use confidence language matched to actual support.

examples.bad:
Claim: Perception robustness is acceptable.
Evidence:
- Simulation report SIM-04.
- Road test report RTR-07.
examples.good:
Claim: Perception robustness is acceptable for the defined visible-object conditions.
Context: Claim excludes object occlusion cases beyond the tested coverage defined in OCS-02.
Evidence:
- Simulation report SIM-04.
- Road test report RTR-07.
Open Issue: Robustness under severe occlusion remains unresolved and requires additional evidence.

Or, if the objection is addressed rather than excluded:
Evidence: Occlusion test report OTR-03.
Justification: The relevant occlusion challenge is explicitly addressed by the added evidence.
examples.problem: The branch presents supporting evidence, but does not make visible that occlusion behavior is only partly covered and remains a relevant challenge to the claim.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case is easier to review and trust when it shows not only supporting material, but also the important limits and challenges that affect confidence in the claim.
review_prompts: Are important limitations visible at the point where they affect the claim?
Are plausible objections or challenges addressed explicitly?
Is unresolved doubt hidden, or made visible through scope restriction, assumptions, monitoring, or open issues?
guidelines.short_rule: Make limitations, objections, and their responses visible where the claim is read.
guidelines.statement: Make relevant limitations, plausible objections, and uncertainty sources explicit, together with how they are addressed in the argument.
guidelines.title: Make limitations, objections, and responses explicit

detection_hints: Look for claims with no visible limitation, exclusion, or open issue despite known partial coverage.

repair.statement: State the limitation as context where the claim is read.
Record the objection as an explicit challenge element.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether known limitations and objections are visible at the point of the affected claim.

examples.bad: A world-class, cutting-edge safety architecture delivers outstanding assurance.
examples.good: The architecture prevents hazardous actuation for fault classes F1-F4 under assumptions A1-A3.
examples.problem: The wording uses promotional adjectives intended to impress the reader rather than to make a reviewable claim; removing the promotional language would lose nothing argumentative.

guidelines.rationale: Safety arguments should build confidence through explicit claims, reasoning, and evidence, not through language intended to impress the reader.
review_prompts: Does the wording sound promotional rather than argumentative?
Would the sentence lose nothing important if the praise-like wording were removed?
Is the wording trying to create confidence through tone rather than support?
guidelines.short_rule: Use no promotional language; persuade through structure and evidence.
guidelines.statement: Do not use promotional, boastful, or image-enhancing language in the safety case.
guidelines.title: Avoid promotional and inflated language

detection_hints: Look for promotional adjectives such as world-class, cutting-edge, outstanding, best-in-class.

repair.statement: Remove the promotional wording and state what is achieved, for what, under which conditions.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether claims use promotional or image-enhancing language. Candidate when a promotional term appears in any element text.

examples.bad: It was determined that the claim is adequately supported.
examples.good: Safety review board SRB-02 reviewed evidence E12-E19 and concluded that the claim is adequately supported.
examples.problem: The passive wording hides who performed the determination; the reviewer cannot identify the responsible actor or hold the judgment to account.

guidelines.rationale: When a review, judgment, approval, or decision is stated without naming who performed it, accountability becomes harder to inspect and challenge.
review_prompts: Who performed the review, judgment, or approval?
Does the wording hide who is responsible?
Would naming the actor improve traceability or auditability?
guidelines.short_rule: Name the actor who performed a review, judgment, or approval.
guidelines.statement: Do not use passive wording when the identity of the actor matters to understanding, reviewing, or challenging the argument.
guidelines.title: Avoid passive voice when it hides agency

detection_hints: Look for it was determined / has been reviewed / is considered without a named actor.

repair.statement: Name the actor who performed the review, judgment, or approval.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether reviews, judgments, and approvals name the responsible actor. Candidate when an agentless passive marker appears and no actor is named in the same element.

examples.bad:
Claim: Perception robustness is acceptable.
Evidence: Perception validation report PVR-08.
A later appendix states that the reported results exclude heavy rain, dense fog, and severe occlusion.
examples.good:
Claim: Perception robustness is acceptable for the validated visibility conditions.
Context: Claim excludes heavy rain, dense fog, and severe occlusion beyond the tested range defined in PVR-08.
Evidence: Perception validation report PVR-08.

Or, where the dependency is really an assumption:
Claim: Perception robustness is acceptable.
Assumption: Visibility conditions remain within the validated range defined in PVR-08.
Evidence: Perception validation report PVR-08.
examples.problem: The main claim appears broad, but important limiting conditions are only visible outside the main branch; a reviewer reading only the claim would be misled about its scope.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case should make important boundaries visible where the claim is read. If key limitations or assumptions are easy to miss, the claim can appear stronger or broader than the argument really supports.
review_prompts: Is an important limitation easy to miss?
Is an important assumption stated explicitly as an assumption, or only implied elsewhere?
Would a reviewer be misled by reading only the main branch?
Should the limitation or dependency be made visible through context, an assumption, or a narrower claim?
guidelines.short_rule: Keep important limitations and assumptions attached to the claim they qualify.
guidelines.statement: Do not hide important limitations or assumptions in appendices, footnotes, or free text that is not directly connected to the claim they qualify.
guidelines.title: Do not bury important limitations or hidden assumptions

detection_hints: Look for important limiting conditions stated only in appendices or distant free text.

repair.statement: Move the buried limitation into context attached to the claim it qualifies.
Move a buried dependency into an assumption attached to the claim.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether important limitations and assumptions are visible where the claim is read. Candidate when a limitation is stated only in a distant location marker rather than attached to the claim it qualifies.

recommendations.recommendation: Apply the full SCCG set. Interpret claims as GSN goals, inference or decomposition steps as strategies, context as GSN context, assumptions as GSN assumptions, and evidence as GSN solutions.

Apply the full SCCG set, but interpret GSN-oriented terms through CAE concepts. Interpret claims as CAE claims, inference or decomposition steps as CAE arguments or warrants, and evidence as CAE evidence or supporting information.

Apply the notation-neutral guideline text first. Use tool guidance only as mapping guidance into the tool's specific element model. Map the tool's own element types onto the notation-neutral element_role values published with the selectable elements, and present SCCG element names in the notation the user sees.

method_application_guidance.summary: SCCG guidelines should be interpreted as notation-neutral quality expectations where possible. When a development process uses a specific assurance-case notation or method, apply the guideline through the corresponding notation elements and make any method-specific interpretation explicit in the guideline text, example, or tool guidance.

prechecks.description: Detects candidate cases where a claim is decomposed without an explicit reasoning step.
prechecks.display_name: Claim has children but no explicit reasoning step
prechecks.fires_when: The selected claim has at least one supporting child element and no strategy or reasoning element between the claim and those children. It does not fire on a strategy that has no children; that is a different defect and is not this pre-check.
prechecks.interpretation: Candidate finding only; reviewer or AI judgment is still required.

prechecks.description: Detects candidate cases where a claim has no path to evidence and is not intentionally undeveloped.
prechecks.fires_when: No descendant of the selected claim is an evidence element, and the claim is not marked undeveloped.
prechecks.interpretation: Candidate finding only; reviewer or AI judgment is still required.

prechecks.description: Detects candidate cases where an evidence element cites a broad artifact without a precise location.
prechecks.fires_when: The selected evidence element names an artifact but neither its text nor the evidence item's cited_section identifies a section, clause, table, figure, dataset, or test identifier within it.
prechecks.interpretation: Candidate finding only; reviewer or AI judgment is still required.

prechecks.description: Detects evidence references without useful control attributes such as owner, version, status, date, or location.
prechecks.fires_when: The evidence item carries none of owner, version, status, date, or location, and no such attribute is stated in the selected evidence element's text. The result names which of those fields are missing.
prechecks.interpretation: Candidate finding only; reviewer or AI judgment is still required.

prechecks.description: Detects evidence references that appear to point to mutable live documents without a fixed version.
prechecks.fires_when: The evidence reference carries a mutable-source marker (see the EV.8 markers) and carries no fixing marker such as a revision, version, snapshot, or capture date.
prechecks.interpretation: Candidate finding only; reviewer or AI judgment is still required.

optional.rationale: Metadata for terminal evidence helps confirm that the traced support is precise and controlled where the claim's credibility depends on the cited artifact (EV.1, EV.3).
Coverage, thresholds, scenarios, and limitations help judge whether the evidence is sufficient for the claim's scope, not merely relevant (LF.5, LF.7, SU.6, SU.8).
Controlled definitions of terms such as safe, acceptable, nominal, or ODD resolve apparent ambiguity or overloaded wording (CL.4, AR.6).

Linked standard requirements help confirm that decomposition or scope claims that appeal to a standard are grounded rather than vague (AR.6), and that reused safety credit is tied to a real conformance basis (SU.5).

Prior findings, review comments, and baseline state show whether the claim has been challenged, whether reused credit still applies (SU.5), and whether monitoring or open-issue commitments exist (SU.4, SU.11).

required.rationale: The selected claim is the subject of the whole review. Its wording drives CL.1, CL.2, CL.3, CL.4, CL.5, CL.6, RD.2, RD.4, and LF.6, and its scope drives every structural, evidential, and sufficiency check applied to the claim.
The parent claim or reasoning step is needed to check that the claim preserves inherited scope and terminology (AR.5), still supports the branch above it, and does not merely restate it (LF.1).
Child elements are the decomposition and first support step below the claim. They are required for CL.2, CL.6, AR.4, LF.1, and LF.2, and to check whether evidence is attached at the correct level.

The connecting strategy or reasoning element shows whether the inference is made explicit rather than inferred from wording (AR.1) and whether support adds independent reasoning rather than restating the claim (LF.1); its absence is itself a finding.

Context, assumptions, and justifications attached to the claim determine whether scope, definitions, and dependencies are externalized rather than hidden in the claim text (CL.3, AR.3, AR.6, AR.7, RD.1, RD.6) and whether limitations are visible where the claim is read (RD.3, SU.9).
Scope and assumptions carried down from ancestors bound how broad or absolute the claim may be (CL.5, AR.5, RD.6) and reveal hidden or contradicted limitations under SU.9.

The path from the claim to its evidence is required to judge traceable support (EV.1), correct claim subject (EV.3), premise relevance (LF.2), representativeness (LF.5), and omission of expected or contrary evidence (LF.7, SU.6, SU.8).

review_profiles.description: Complete review of a selected claim (goal), covering wording, context, decomposition, evidence support, reasoning soundness, and sufficiency.

optional.rationale: Inherited scope and assumptions help confirm that the strategy does not silently override ancestor terminology or boundaries (AR.2 consistency).
The descendant evidence path is useful when the reasoning relies on undocumented system knowledge (EV.9) or leaves plausible challenges to the decomposition unaddressed (SU.1).
The glossary resolves project-specific decomposition categories, functions, hazards, or ODD terms used in the reasoning rule.
Standard links help verify that a decomposition claiming to follow a standard or external structure is grounded rather than a vague appeal to authority (AR.2).
Prior findings and review comments reveal whether plausible challenges to the reasoning step have already been raised and left unaddressed (SU.1).

required.rationale: The selected strategy or reasoning element is the object of review. AR.1 and AR.2 require it to make the inference rule explicit, and LF.1 requires checking that it adds independent support rather than restating the parent.
A strategy can only be judged against the claim it supports. AR.2 asks whether it explains how the parent is decomposed or argued, and LF.1 whether the reasoning merely restates the parent.
The supporting elements are needed to judge whether the reasoning rule actually produces this child set and whether the decomposition is complete, relevant, and non-circular (AR.2, LF.1).
Strategies rely on local scope, decomposition criteria, and dependencies that must be visible to decide whether the reasoning is valid for the branch (AR.1, AR.2).

review_profiles.description: Complete review of a selected strategy or reasoning step, covering whether the inference between the parent claim and its supporting claims is explicit and sound.

optional.rationale: The claim's local scope and assumptions define what the evidence must cover and help detect evidence that is relevant to a neighboring or broader claim but not sufficient here (LF.2, EV.5).
The path from claim to this evidence helps confirm traceable support and correct attachment level, especially where intermediate claims are skipped (EV.1, LF.2).
The glossary resolves controlled terms used in the artifact or its acceptance criteria so the evidence is interpreted consistently.
Standard links confirm that an evidence type or acceptance criterion that appeals to a standard is grounded rather than assumed (EV.2, EV.5).
Prior findings, review comments, and baseline state identify unstable, challenged, stale, or dismissed evidence (EV.7, EV.8, SU.1, SU.6).

required.rationale: The selected solution or evidence reference is the element under review. It identifies which artifact is cited and what role it plays, which is the basis for AR.1, EV.1, and RD.1.

Artifact metadata such as type, owner, version, date, status, location, and cited section is required to judge whether the evidence type is reviewable and the citation precise, controlled, and stable (EV.2, EV.4, EV.7, EV.8).

Scope, coverage, thresholds, scenarios, configurations, and limitations are required to judge sufficiency and inferential fit rather than citation hygiene alone (EV.5, EV.6, LF.5, LF.7, SU.3, SU.6, SU.7, SU.8).
The claim the evidence supports is required to judge relevance to the immediate claim (LF.2), a correct and traceable evidence path (EV.1), and whether the inferential link is explained (EV.6).

review_profiles.description: Complete review of a selected evidence item (solution), covering reviewability, control, citation precision, sufficiency, and inferential fit to the supported claim.

when_absent.statement: Without an evidence basis the review can judge citation, control, and element role, but not whether the evidence is sufficient for the claim. Report the remaining findings, state that sufficiency was not assessed, and do not report an absent basis as a finding against the argument.

optional.rationale: The scope and argument location the assumption qualifies help decide whether it is local, should be inherited more broadly, or should be converted into a claim that requires support (SU.9).
Prior findings and baseline state show whether the assumption is monitored, has been challenged, or needs a defined re-assessment trigger (SU.2, SU.4).
Controlled definitions help judge whether the assumption is specific enough to be checked, challenged, and monitored (SU.10).

required.rationale: The selected assumption is the dependency under review. SU.2, SU.9, SU.10, AR.3, AR.7, and RD.6 require checking whether it is explicit, bounded, monitorable, and correctly placed, while AR.1 and RD.1 check that it is used and signposted for its role.
Assumptions and justifications attached at the selected point expose the reasonableness basis, the monitoring expectation, and whether the condition should instead be context or a claim (SU.2, SU.9).
Assumptions often propagate from ancestors, so inherited context is required to detect conflicts, over-broad inherited dependencies, or limitations otherwise hidden from the branch (RD.6, SU.10).

review_profiles.description: Complete review of a selected assumption, covering whether it is explicit, bounded, correctly placed, monitorable, and not hiding an unsupported claim.

optional.rationale: When the justification explains a decomposition or inference choice, the strategy shows whether it is local rationale for that step or is trying to carry the argument itself (AR.8, AR.9).
The evidence path helps detect rationale used as hidden support, arguments from ignorance, and low-risk claims resting only on simulation or uneventful operation (AR.8, LF.3, SU.7).

When the justification cites expert review, prior practice, or proven-in-use evidence, artifact metadata shows whether the cited basis is controlled and reviewable rather than unsupported opinion (SU.3, SU.5).
Coverage, thresholds, and comparison basis help judge sufficiency appeals and unjustified comparisons or distinctions (EV.5, LF.4, SU.7).

Prior review comments, unresolved findings, and baseline shifts show whether the justification has been challenged, whether agency is clear (RD.5), and whether reused safety credit still applies (SU.5).

required.rationale: The selected justification or warrant is the object of review. AR.8, AR.9, EV.5, SU.3, SU.5, LF.3, LF.4, RD.1, and RD.5 all require inspecting what the rationale actually says and whether it names the responsible actor.

A justification can only be judged against the element or inference it is attached to. AR.8 asks whether it replaces evidence or argument, and AR.9 whether it explains this exact parent rather than a different issue elsewhere in the branch.

review_profiles.description: Complete review of a selected justification or warrant, covering whether it explains local rationale without replacing needed argument or evidence.

optional.rationale: Ancestor scope and assumptions show whether this context is consistent with, or silently narrows or contradicts, inherited limits (RD.6, SU.9).
Controlled definitions confirm that terms introduced or relied on by the context are used consistently across the branch (AR.6).
When the context cites external standards or operating constraints, standard links help verify the reference is relevant and not used as vague or hidden context (AR.3).

required.rationale: The selected context element is the object of review. AR.1, AR.3, AR.6, AR.7, RD.1, and RD.3 require checking whether it is used for its role and whether it supplies clear scope, definitions, and operating conditions.

The claim or element the context qualifies is required to judge whether the context is sufficient and relevant for interpreting that claim (AR.6), whether scope and dependencies are correctly externalized to it (AR.3, AR.7), and whether limitations are visible where the claim is read (RD.3, RD.6).

review_profiles.description: Complete review of a selected context element, covering whether it provides sufficient, relevant, and consistent scope and definitions for the claim it qualifies.

optional.rationale: Supporting elements added in response show whether the challenge was resolved by added evidence, a narrowed claim, or new assumptions and monitoring (SU.11).
Context and assumptions attached to the challenge or its target help judge whether the challenge is in scope and how its resolution constrains the affected claim (SU.11).
Review comments, prior findings, and proposal history show whether the challenge was rejected, sustained, or left as a visible and traceable open issue (SU.11).

required.rationale: The selected counter claim or defeater is the challenge under review. SU.11 requires checking whether the challenge is stated explicitly as a distinct element rather than left in review comments or reviewer intuition.
The claim, reasoning step, or evidence being challenged is required to judge whether the challenge is relevant to its target and whether the branch has been updated to resolve it (SU.11).

review_profiles.description: Complete review of a selected counter claim or defeater, covering whether the challenge is stated explicitly and carried to a visible resolution.
